# Kāyagatāsati Sutta (MN 119 (PTS MN iii 88))
**ID:** MN 119 (PTS MN iii 88)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Kāyagatāsati Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Mindfulness of the Body
**PTS:** MN iii 88
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn119
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kāyagatāsati Sutta* (MN 119, PTS MN iii 88) is a discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* dedicated entirely to the cultivation and benefits of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatā sati*) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2014]. In sutta usage, *kāyagatā sati* broadly encompasses all meditation exercises based on the physical body, unlike the later commentarial tradition which often restricts the term specifically to contemplation of the thirty-two bodily parts [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2012]. The text presents an array of bodily contemplations—beginning with the first four steps of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*), bodily postures, clear comprehension, anatomical parts, elements, and charnel-ground meditations—and notably includes the attainment of the four absorptions (*jhāna*), highlighting the physical experience and bodily pervasive bliss accompanying these meditative absorptions [Anālayo 2003; Anālayo 2019; Polak 2011]. A recurring refrain emphasizes how the mind settles, becomes concentrated, and sheds worldly memories and intentions through each practice, leading to numerous beneficial qualities and mental detachment [Shulman 2014; Anālayo 2014].
Computational text-reuse analysis confirms massive shared passages across early Buddhist corpora, showing extensive alignment with the *Pañcakanipāta* (AN 5.28 on the fivefold samādhi), DN 22, MN 20, MN 39, DN 2, and SN 54, as well as cross-language matches with Chinese āgamas (T 26, T 125, T 1) and Sanskrit works such as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
